title: Easy to remember
hookLine: We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; is there any who will remember (54:17)
carry: is there any who will remember?

lines: THE MOON SURAH HAS A CHORUS.
cards: Someone reads you a phone number once. A minute later it's gone. But the chorus of a song you haven't heard in ten years is still there, every word, back the moment the first note plays.
Some words stick. Surah fifty-four, the Moon, tells one hard story after another: Nuh and the flood, the people of 'Ad and the wind, Thamud and the she-camel, the people of Lut.
And between the stories, like a chorus, one line keeps coming back. It's about remembering, and it ends with a question.

teach.b: Pickthall: "And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?"
The line returns, almost word for word, in verses twenty-two, thirty-two and forty: four times, each after a story closes. The Arabic for we have made it easy is yassarna, from the root y-s-r, ease.
And remembering is dhikr, the remembrance this path has met so often. Classical commentators read the verse two ways at once. Easy to remember: the Qur'an is easy to hold in memory.
And easy for remembrance: easy to take a reminder from. The first reading is lived out.

teach.h: A HAFIZ KEEPS THE WHOLE BOOK.
teach.b: Children and adults memorize the entire book, and someone who has done it is called a hafiz, a keeper or guardian of it. Some do it before Arabic is their everyday language, with a teacher listening line by line.
But the verse doesn't stop at the ease. It ends on a question: fa hal min muddakir, so is there anyone who will remember? The ease is offered; someone has to pick it up.
And a hadith in Bukhari adds a kindness for those who find it hard.

teach.h: A DOUBLE REWARD FOR THE ONE WHO STRUGGLES.
teach.b: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said the one skilled in the Qur'an will be with the noble scribes, and the one who struggles, reciting with difficulty, has a double reward. So the question isn't only for the gifted.
It's put to anyone with one verse they could learn.

how: Many Muslims memorize short surahs as children for the daily prayers, and some memorize the whole Qur'an with a teacher who listens line by line; a person who has done so is called a hafiz.

o: a prayer said only inside the mosque
remembrance, keeping God and His word in mind
the act of memorizing the whole Qur'an

games.q: the chorus of the Moon — tap the pairs.
p: one who holds the whole book

s: the 'easy to remember' line appears only once in Surah Al-Qamar
it comes back four times: verses 17, 22, 32 and 40, each after a story.
someone who has memorized the whole Qur'an is called a hafiz
a keeper or guardian of the book.
the hadith says only the skilled reciter is rewarded
the one who recites with difficulty has a double reward.

games.q: you're learning a verse and you keep stumbling over it. according to the hadith in Bukhari, where does that leave you?
o: better to stop until it comes easily.
games.why: the Prophet said the one who struggles, reciting with difficulty, has a double reward; the effort itself counts.

practice: If you're Muslim, take a verse you half-know, maybe the opening of Surah Al-Ikhlas, and say it slowly, again and again, until it holds without looking.
If that isn't yours, say today's line on the out-breath a few times: is there any that remembereth? Then stop, and see whether it stays with you in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Dhikr: remembrance, the word behind Surah Al-Qamar's chorus that the Qur'an was made easy to hold onto, asking four times who will take it up. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: so is there anyone who will remember? The question that closes the chorus of Surah Al-Qamar.

carryVoice: Your line: is there any who will remember? The week climbed from the Mount and the fading stars, through the Star and its lote tree, to the split moon and today's chorus. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And in truth We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; but is there any that remembereth?

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4937; Sahih Muslim 798 (the skilled reciter and the one who struggles)
